title: Guru Amar Das's gurpurab
hook: remembered at Goindval, the well of eighty-four steps

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurmukhi, and your line: the script and the kitchen. It ends a week that closed the shabads for a life, began the month at Sangrand, looked up at the full moon, talked kindly about dates, and visited the city of the pool. Today, a well. Day six hundred eighty-six.
screen: `A HYMN FOR EVERY TURN · THE MONTH BEGINS · FULL MOON · DATES · THE POOL · THE SCRIPT AND THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Here's a life that runs the other way from the usual story of starting young. Tradition remembers a man who spent most of his life as a devout pilgrim of his own tradition, walking to the Ganges again and again. Then, already old, he hears a young woman singing Guru Nanak's hymns while she churns butter, and everything changes. Years later, past seventy, tradition says, he becomes the third Guru. Today: baoli.
screen: `A LIFE THAT STARTS LATE.` → `A LIFETIME A PILGRIM.` → `A SONG AT THE BUTTER CHURN.`

segments.voice: The young woman singing at the churn was Bibi Amro, Guru Angad's daughter, married into his family. Tradition says he was so moved that he went to Khadur, and for years served Guru Angad: carrying water from the river before dawn, every day. He became Guru, tradition says, past seventy. He settled at Goindval, on the river Beas, and two things there are remembered on his gurpurab. The first is the langar. Tradition says he asked everyone who came to eat in the free kitchen first, sitting together on the floor, before meeting him: high caste and low, rich and poor, side by side. Sikhs remember a saying linked to him: first the pangat, the row of people eating, then the sangat, the gathering. The second is the baoli, a stepwell. He had a deep well built at Goindval, with steps leading down to the water: eighty-four of them. Water open to everyone, with no caste rule at the bottom. Today some pilgrims walk down to the water reciting the Japji Sahib once on each step, a long, slow devotion. Some Sikhs connect the eighty-four steps to the old Indian idea of eighty-four lakh lives; others keep it simply as a practice of patience, and some point out that Gurbani speaks of liberation by grace and the Name, not by counting. Either way, it's a picture of the third Guru himself: going down, step by step, slowly, toward water.
screen: `A PILGRIM, AND A SONG AT THE CHURN.` · `PANGAT FIRST, THEN SANGAT.` · `THE BAOLI AT GOINDVAL.` · `ONE JAPJI ON EACH STEP.` · then, large: `EIGHTY-FOUR STEPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drink water slowly. Pour a glass of water and sit with it. Look at it first. Think of the people at Goindval, walking down eighty-four steps to reach it. Then drink, in small sips, slowly, noticing the cool of it, the way it goes down. Between sips, breathe. Let the glass take the whole length of the bell if it can. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each sip. The bell holds the time.
Baoli, the stepwell of eighty-four steps Guru Amar Das built at Goindval, remembered along with the langar where all sat together.
Your line: eighty-four steps. Today, take one task you've been rushing and go down into it slowly, one step at a time. Day six hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: On Guru Amar Das's gurpurab, gurdwaras hold kirtan and langar, and at Goindval Sahib some pilgrims descend the baoli, reciting Japji Sahib on each of its eighty-four steps.
